prize_parts.citation: For a poetic and essayistic oeuvre that renews the lyric through hybrid forms, joining classical antiquity, translation, grief and desire in a voice of rare formal daring and intellectual depth.

statement.case_for: After reading my colleagues' openings I keep Carson first, on the strength of her voice and formal achievement rather than on how many members rank her highly. Autobiography of Red recasts the Geryon myth as a verse novel, and Nox builds an elegy from translation, archive and the book as object. In both, the formal invention carries real emotional and intellectual weight. The same preoccupations recur across a long body of work that includes essays such as Eros the Bittersweet, verse collections such as Plainwater, Men in the Off Hours and Decreation, and later hybrid books. This is sustained development, not one gesture. Her scholarly and philological rigor is part of the poetry's making, not a separate activity beside it. The whole-oeuvre test is met by a recognizable and continually renewed way of making poems and prose that treats the boundaries between genres as material. The citation I propose stresses the original poetry and essays and treats translation as part of the same practice. That keeps the scope within one named writer.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that Carson's reach depends on page design, allusion and her relation to Greek and Latin texts, and these may not survive translation into other languages. If so, a committee reading in translation would be judging a partial image. A second concern is whether her corpus is concentrated and fragmentary enough that the weight falls on a handful of books, notably Autobiography of Red and Nox. A third is whether the hybrid, scholarly mode answers to what Nobel's will describes as literature of an idealistic direction, or is better understood as a brilliant scholarly-poetic achievement. I regard these as real risks. They are not yet reasons to prefer another candidate, but they would weigh more if colleagues who read the work more closely found the later books mannered.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for a hard-to-mistake voice and sustained imaginative depth, and puts Carson second, noting that some of Carson's work is material and visual (Nox as an object) and that it is unclear whether translation and adaptation belong to the core achievement.
responses.response: I agree that Cărtărescu's voice and metaphysical scale are very strong, and I rank him second. I also accept that the material dimension of Nox does not reduce to text on a page. But Nox is a case where the book-object is the form of the elegy and not an add-on. The text still works through the fragmentary translation of Catullus 101 and the poet's address to her brother. On translation, I would keep the citation anchored in the original poetry and essays, so the core case never depends on whether her versions of Greek texts count. My doubt about Cărtărescu is narrower. A great deal of his effect lies in the sentence-level density of Romanian, which I cannot judge in translation, and the case rests on a few very large novels. The two cases are close, and I would not call the choice between them settled.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg, who ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson second, asks how much of Carson's oeuvre is original creation as against translation and adaptation, and whether the formal play is sustained or sometimes mannered.
responses.response: I think the first question is fair, and my answer is that the case should be made on the original works. Eros the Bittersweet, Autobiography of Red, Plainwater, The Beauty of the Husband, Nox and the later hybrid books are original and carry the achievement. The versions of Sappho and Greek drama belong to the same imaginative world but do not need to bear the argument. On mannerism, I concede that some later books are more occasional and that experiments of this kind can slide into erudite play. I would answer that the best work shows formal risk serving feeling and not the reverse, and that is the evidence I rely on. I have not independently checked every later book, so this is a point where a closer reader on the committee could correct me.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first but notes that the formal radicalism sometimes sits at the edge of what is conventionally read as a literary genre, and that the corpus is smaller and more fragmentary than that of many novelists.
responses.response: I share this reservation and listed a related one in my own opening. I would add that fragmentation here is a method with a long lineage in lyric and philology and not a deficiency of range. Concentrated work can meet the whole-oeuvre standard if its quality holds across decades, which is the question I think the committee should test book by book. I would not accept that bulk is a literary criterion in its own right. Where I agree with Carlberg is that the citation must name both the poetry and the essayistic and translational practice, or it will misdescribe the achievement. My proposed citation tries to do that without widening the credit beyond one writer.

uncertainties: How much of Carson's effect survives in translation, particularly in languages other than English, and how much depends on typography, layout and the visual or material design of the books.
Whether the later books (after roughly 2010) keep the level of the 1990s and 2000s work. My view rests on general public knowledge and not on a fresh reading.

Whether a committee member reading in translation can fairly judge Cărtărescu's Romanian sentence texture, Tawada's two-language corpus or Adonis's Arabic prosody against Carson's English, and so whether the comparison is evenly informed.
Whether the hybrid scholarly-poetic mode fits the 'idealistic direction' in Nobel's will, as Carlberg and I both flagged.
I have not independently verified any source or read the full corpus of any shortlisted writer.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. Her shared first name with the candidate is coincidental and is not a connection, and her profile records no relationship with any shortlisted writer.
